options: An event is processed zero or one times — a failure at the wrong moment (e.g., committing before processing finishes) loses it entirely
An event is always processed at least twice
An event can never be lost under any circumstances
It requires a transactional producer and consumer to work at all
questions.explain: At-most-once is fire-and-forget: no retry on the producer side, or committing the consumer's offset before handle() actually runs.

questions.q: Why can at-least-once delivery produce duplicate processing?
options: Retries (producer resending after a lost ack, or a consumer re-reading after crashing before commit) can reprocess the same event
At-least-once always drops every second event on purpose
Duplicates only happen with at-most-once, never at-least-once
Kafka physically stores two copies of every event in every partition
questions.explain: Retrying until acknowledged, and committing only after processing succeeds, closes the data-loss gap but opens the door to duplicates.

questions.q: Why is at-least-once considered the common default in real systems, per this lesson?
options: It never silently loses data, and duplicates can be designed around with an idempotent handle() function
It's the only delivery semantic Kafka actually supports
It's always faster than at-most-once in every case
It requires no configuration of any kind
questions.explain: Losing data silently is usually worse than an occasional duplicate that idempotent processing logic can absorb harmlessly.

questions.q: What does an idempotent producer actually do to make exactly-once real?
options: The broker tracks a producer ID and sequence number per partition, so it can detect and discard a retried duplicate write
It simply never retries a failed write, accepting possible loss instead
It writes every event to two different topics as a backup
It disables all consumer groups reading that topic
questions.explain: This producer ID + sequence number tracking is the actual mechanism, not just a configuration flag with no real behavior behind it.

questions.q: What's a real limitation of Kafka's exactly-once guarantee?
options: It only covers the Kafka-to-Kafka hop — a write to something outside Kafka (a database, an API) still needs its own idempotency handling
It has no limitations and covers every system a pipeline ever touches
It only works if the topic has exactly one partition
It eliminates the need for a consumer group entirely
questions.explain: Idempotent producers and transactions are genuine, but they don't extend Kafka's guarantee past its own boundary into external systems.
